rubric.why: Identifies the larger quantity requirement and gives a macronutrient example.
rubric.description: Macronutrients are minerals required in larger quantities, with an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when the answer gives the larger-quantity requirement and at least one example.

rubric.why: Identifies the lower quantity requirement and gives a micronutrient example.
rubric.description: Micronutrients are minerals required in lower quantities, with an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when the answer gives the lower-quantity requirement and at least one example.

modelAnswer: The minerals which are required in larger quantities are called macronutrients e.g. carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, potassium, nitrogen, sulphur, calcium, and magnesium. The minerals which are required in lower quantities are called micronutrients e.g. iron, molybdenum, boron, copper, manganese, zinc, chlorine, and nickel.

rubric.why: States the defining loss of water from the plant surface in vapour form.
rubric.description: Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from a plant surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water loss as vapour from the plant surface.

rubric.why: Names the three types or the three plant structures through which they occur.
rubric.description: Names stomatal, cuticular, and lenticular transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when all three types (or their corresponding structures) are named.

modelAnswer: The loss of water in the form of vapours from plant surface is called transpiration. This loss may occur through stomata in leaves, through the cuticle present on leaf epidermis, or through special openings called lenticels present in the stems of some plants. The three types are stomatal transpiration, cuticular transpiration, and lenticular transpiration.

rubric.why: Identifies the pull created by transpiration on water columns in xylem.
rubric.description: Transpiration creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that transpiration pulls on water columns in xylem.

rubric.why: States the result and direction of the pull: transport of water and salts from roots to leaves.
rubric.description: The pull transports water and salts from root to leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when water and salts are both identified as transported from root to leaves.

modelAnswer: Although transpiration is the loss of water from plant but, yet it creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem tissue of leaves, stem and root. This pull is responsible for the transport of water and salts from root to leaves.

rubric.why: Gives the textbook conclusion that transpiration is a necessary evil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying transpiration as a necessary evil.

rubric.why: Explains its importance through the xylem pull that transports water and salts from roots to leaves.
rubric.description: Transpiration creates a pull on xylem water columns, transporting water and salts from root to leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when the answer connects the xylem pull with transport of water and salts from root to leaves.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is a necessary evil. Although transpiration is the loss of water from plant but, yet it creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem tissue of leaves, stem and root. This pull is responsible for the transport of water and salts from root to leaves.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water and salts as the materials transported by xylem.
Award 1 mark for identifying food as the material transported by phloem.

modelAnswer: Xylem is responsible for the transport of water and salts while phloem is responsible for the transport of food.

rubric.why: Identifies latex as the waste excreted by the rubber plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for matching the rubber plant with latex.

rubric.why: Identifies gums as the waste excreted by the keekar (Acacia) tree.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for matching keekar or Acacia with gums.

modelAnswer: For example, rubber plant excretes latexes, Acacia (keekar) tree excretes gums.
